hook.support: You tell a mate something big. They keep scrolling. They say “yeah, yeah”. How does that feel? Now think of someone who **really** listens. You can tell straight away.
hook.core: You’re telling a mate something that matters. They keep scrolling and say “yeah, yeah”. You stop talking. Now think of someone who **really** listens: they look up, they wait, they ask the next question. You can tell the difference in seconds.
hook.extend: You’re telling a friend something that matters. They nod, scroll, and say “yeah, yeah”. You give up halfway. Now picture someone who **really** listens: they put the phone down, let you finish, and ask exactly the right follow-up question. Listening isn’t silence. It’s a skill other people can see.

why.support: Good listeners get better jobs, better mates and better help. At work, at the doctor, in a group, listening is how you get the facts right.
why.core: Listening is a skill you use every day: at work, at the doctor, at Centrelink, in a group. Good listeners get the facts right the first time, make people feel heard, and ask the questions that keep a conversation going.
why.extend: Listening is how you get information, show respect and build trust. Employers rank it near the top of the skills they want. In a discussion, the person who listens best usually asks the question that moves everyone forward.

articles.title: Listening you can see

body.support:
Listening is not just being quiet. People can **see** if you are listening. Good listeners use four moves.

1. **Face it.** Put your phone down. Turn to the person. Look at them.
2. **Let them finish.** Don’t cut in. When they stop, wait two seconds. They often say more.
3. **Say it back.** Use your own words. “So the bus didn’t come at all?” Now they know you got it.
4. **Ask more.** Ask **open** questions. These start with *what*, *how*, *why* or *tell me*.

A **closed** question gets a short answer. “Was it good?” “Yeah.”

An **open** question gets a story. “What was the best part?”

A **follow-up** builds on their answer. “Why was that the best part?”

Use these moves with friends, at work, and with a doctor.
body.core:
Listening isn’t just staying quiet. People can **see** whether you’re listening, and it changes how much they tell you. Good listeners use four moves.

1. **Face it.** Phone down, body turned towards them, eyes on them most of the time. A nod or “mm” shows you’re still with them.
2. **Let them finish.** Don’t jump in with your own story. When they stop, wait two seconds. People often add the most important part after a pause.
3. **Say it back.** Put what they said into your own words: “So you got the shift, but nobody told you the start time?” This is called **paraphrasing**. It shows you understood, and it lets them fix anything you got wrong.
4. **Ask more.** Ask questions that open the conversation up.

**Closed questions** get short answers: “Was it good?” “Yeah.” They’re useful for checking a fact.

**Open questions** start with *what*, *how*, *why* or *tell me about*. They get stories: “What was the hardest part?”

**Follow-up questions** build on the answer you just got: “You said it was hard. What made it hard?” They prove you were listening.

The four moves work everywhere: with a mate who’s having a bad day, in a job interview, in a group discussion, or with a doctor.
body.extend:
Listening isn’t the gap between your turns to talk. It’s an active skill, and the people around you can see it. Good listeners use four moves.

1. **Face it.** Phone away, body turned towards the speaker, steady but relaxed eye contact. Small signals such as a nod or “mm” tell them to keep going.
2. **Let them finish.** Resist jumping in with your own story or advice. When they stop, wait a couple of seconds: people often add the most important detail after a pause.
3. **Say it back.** **Paraphrase** what you heard: “So you got the shift, but nobody told you the start time?” This checks your understanding and gives them the chance to correct it.
4. **Ask more.** Choose your questions on purpose.

**Closed questions** (“Did you finish?”) get short answers. Use them to check a fact.

**Open questions** (“What happened when you got there?”) invite a story.

**Follow-up questions** (“You said it felt unfair. What would have made it fair?”) build on the last answer, which is the clearest proof you were listening.

Your **tone** matters too. The same question can sound curious or like an interrogation. Match your questions and tone to the person and the situation: a friend who’s upset needs gentler questions than a manager giving instructions.

caseStudies.title: The 11-second doctor

body.support:
In 2018, researchers watched **112** recorded visits to doctors in the United States.

They timed how long patients spoke before the doctor cut in.

Patients were cut off **7 times out of 10**. On average, it happened about **11 seconds** after they started.

The study also found that in only about **one visit in three** did the doctor ask why the patient had come.

That matters. If a doctor cuts in too soon, they might miss the real problem.
body.core:
In 2018, a team of researchers studied **112** recorded visits between doctors and patients in the United States. They wanted to know one thing: do doctors let patients explain why they came?

The answer surprised a lot of people. Patients were interrupted **7 times out of 10**, on average about **11 seconds** after they started talking. And doctors asked about the patient’s reason for the visit in only about **a third** of visits.

The researchers said a well-timed interruption can help focus a conversation. But cutting in too early means the doctor may miss what’s really worrying the patient.

It works both ways. Going to a doctor? Say your main worry first, and bring a short list.
body.extend:
In 2018, researchers studied **112** recorded visits between doctors and patients in the United States. The study was published in the *Journal of General Internal Medicine*. The team checked two things: did doctors ask why the patient had come, and how long did patients speak before being cut off?

Patients were interrupted **seven times out of ten**, on average about **11 seconds** after they began. Doctors asked about the reason for the visit in only about **a third** of consultations.

The researchers didn’t say every interruption is bad. A respectful question can focus a conversation. Their point was about timing. Cut in too early, and you answer the problem you *expect*, not the real one.

That’s true far beyond medicine. In an interview, a complaint or an argument, the person who waits and asks the right follow-up usually understands the situation best.

source.name: Springer Nature media release — “Wait, just a second, is your doctor listening?” (19 July 2018), on Singh Ospina et al., Journal of General Internal Medicine

model.text:
**Who:** my cousin Ana. **Topic:** her job at the vet clinic.

**My open questions:**
1. What does a normal day look like?
2. What’s the hardest part?
3. How did you get the job?

**Follow-ups I asked:**
- You said the hardest part is upset owners. What do you say to them?
- You did work experience there first. What did you do to stand out?

**I said back:** “So you started with work experience, and they asked you back?”

**Three things I learned:** she cleans cages before 7 am, she uses a calm voice with upset owners, and work experience got her the job.
why: The open questions start with **what** and **how**, so Ana had to tell a story.
Each follow-up uses Ana’s own words, which shows real listening.
The three things learned are specific facts, not “she likes her job”.

teacher.overview: Students learn four visible listening moves (face it, let them finish, say it back, ask more) and three question types (closed, open, follow-up). They annotate a short conversation, convert closed questions to open ones, plan an interview, and interview someone for four minutes while a partner tallies the moves. The case study is a 2018 study of 112 recorded doctor visits in which patients were usually interrupted within about 11 seconds.
prep: Pair students thoughtfully: the interview works best with someone they don’t know well.
Have a list of safe, low-stakes discussion questions ready for the Level Up (e.g. “Should school start later?”).
Optional: role-play a bad listener (phone out, interrupting) for the hook.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — The four moves
steps: **Hook (10 min):** role-play a terrible listener with a volunteer. What did they notice?
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** the four moves; open, closed and follow-up questions.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Questions that work
steps: **Case study (15 min):** the 11-second doctor. Link to students’ own appointments.
**Open it up (10 min):** convert closed questions.
**Plan (15 min):** interview questions; model one plan aloud.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — The interview
steps: **Interviews (20 min):** 4 minutes each way, partners tally.
**Share (10 min):** three things learned about their partner.
**Level Up (10 min):** group discussion with an observer.
**Check & reflect (10 min):** quick check, reflection, sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** stocktake — closed; after the game — open; pain this week — open; dinner at six — closed; tell me more — open; worked in retail — closed.

**Annotation:** 1 face it + open question; 2 let them finish (Jay adds the mistake after a pause); 3 say it back / paraphrase; 4 short answer (fact); 5 open question; 6 follow-up using Jay’s words.

**Case study:** interrupted 7 times out of 10, on average about 11 seconds in; the doctor may miss the real reason for the visit; students: say the main worry first, bring a list, ask “Can I finish?”.

**Open it up (examples):** What do you enjoy about your job? / Which part of the test was hardest? / What are you planning to study at TAFE, and why?

realityCheck: **Pairing matters.** Interviews between close friends turn into chats; between students who clash, they stall. Choose pairs, or let students interview a staff member.
**Some students will freeze on the first question.** The plan page is the safety net: they can read their first question straight off it.
**Eye contact norms vary across cultures**, including for some First Nations students. Teach “face it” as turning towards the person, not as staring.
**Keep topics safe.** Steer interviews away from family conflict, health or anything private. Jobs, hobbies and skills work best.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It’s short, social and the improvement is easy to see in one lesson.
